title: How leadership shapes team performance
blurb: Explain how a project manager's leadership lifts or drags down motivation, morale, commitment and performance, and what good leadership looks like in practice.
question: An online retailer's checkout project is slipping. The project manager has started checking every task personally and criticising mistakes in the daily stand-up. Developers have stopped suggesting improvements and defects are now hidden until testing. How is the leadership affecting performance, and what should the project manager do differently?

teach.h: Leadership: the people side of delivery
teach.body: Formally, leadership is the ability to set vision and direction, to influence and align people towards a common purpose, and to empower and inspire them to achieve success. In plain English: helping people understand where the project is going and why, and making them want to give their best to get there. Leadership affects the team's motivation, morale and commitment, and through those it drives performance: quality, pace, ideas and how early problems are raised.

teach.h: From leader behaviour to project results

teach.caption: The PM rarely changes performance directly. They change the climate, and the climate changes what people choose to give.

teach.h: Leadership and management: a PM needs both
teach.caption: A tidy plan nobody believes in fails; so does enthusiasm with no control. Good project managers do both.

teach.h: Why leadership matters so much on projects
teach.body: Projects are temporary and cross-functional. In a matrix, team members still report to line managers, so the PM often has little formal authority and must lead through influence. The real prize is discretionary effort: the gap between doing the minimum and giving full commitment, ideas and early warnings. Good leadership earns it. Poor leadership costs it, and the consequences are serious: hidden problems, stress, low morale, delays, poor decisions and good people leaving.

teach.caption: Pressure and fear can buy short-term compliance, but not commitment. The bill arrives later as rework and attrition.

teach.h: The levers a project manager controls

children.label: Clarity
children.sub: Clear objectives and the purpose behind them

children.label: Involvement
children.sub: A say in how the work is done

teach.body: Priya leads an iterative checkout rebuild for an online retailer. Under deadline pressure she begins checking every task and naming mistakes in the stand-up. Within two sprints, defects are hidden until testing and nobody suggests improvements. She resets: agrees clear sprint goals with the product owner, explains why checkout matters to customers, thanks people for raising defects early and lets the team decide how to build. Problems now surface daily and velocity recovers.

teach.h: Leading in linear and iterative life cycles
teach.caption: In both, people need clarity, recognition and support. Tight command-and-control clashes most with iterative ways of working.

teach.text: The classic trap: assuming more pressure or tighter control always raises performance. With a capable team, options that 'impose strict control' or 'check every task' usually reduce ownership and hide problems. Also, motivation is not just pay: clarity, involvement, recognition and support do most of the work.

teach.h: How this comes up in a written answer
items: State the link: leadership shapes the team climate, which drives motivation, morale and commitment, and so performance.
Give positive behaviours: clear objectives and purpose, involvement in decisions, specific timely feedback and recognition, removing blockers.
Give consequences of poor leadership: hidden problems, minimum effort, stress, low morale, delays, people leaving.
Tie it to the project: earlier issue reporting, better quality, sustained pace, objectives and benefits protected.
Show judgement: adapt the approach to the team's capability and the life cycle (directing work vs facilitating a self-organising team).
Leadership sets direction, influences and inspires; management plans and controls. A PM needs both.
Leadership drives performance through the climate it creates: motivation, morale and commitment.
Clarity, involvement, feedback, support and appropriate autonomy lift performance.
Blame and over-control buy short-term compliance but hide problems and cost commitment.
In iterative projects the PM facilitates a self-organising team rather than directing tasks.

summary: You can now explain how a project manager's behaviour shapes the team climate and, through motivation, morale and commitment, the team's performance. You can also name the leadership behaviours that lift performance and the consequences when leadership goes wrong.

A.q: Which statement BEST describes the difference between leadership and management on a project?
options: Leadership plans and controls; management inspires people
Leadership inspires and aligns people; management controls
Leadership is for sponsors; management is for project managers
Leadership relies on authority; management relies on trust
A.why: Leadership sets direction, influences and inspires people; management plans, organises and controls the work. A project manager needs both.

whyNot.0: This reverses the two: planning and controlling is management.
whyNot.2: Both sponsors and project managers lead and manage; neither is reserved for one role.
whyNot.3: It is the other way round: leadership relies mainly on influence and trust, management on process and authority.

A.q: Complete the statement: leadership affects project performance mainly because it shapes the team's ____.
options: motivation, morale and commitment
contract terms and pay grades
technical skills and qualifications
job titles and reporting lines
A.why: Leadership creates the climate that drives motivation, morale and commitment, and those drive quality, pace and openness.

whyNot.1: Contract terms and pay grades are set by the organisation and HR, not by day-to-day leadership.
whyNot.2: Skills come mainly from selection, training and experience; leadership affects how willingly they are used.
whyNot.3: Job titles and reporting lines are structural; they don't explain why the same team performs differently under different leaders.

A.q: Which of the following is NOT a likely consequence of poor project leadership?
options: Problems hidden until late
Capable people leaving the team
Earlier escalation of issues
Lower morale and more stress
A.why: Poor leadership makes people less willing to speak up, so issues are raised LATER, not earlier. Earlier escalation is a sign of good leadership.

whyNot.0: Blame and fear lead people to hide problems until formal reviews, a classic consequence.
whyNot.1: Poor leadership is a common reason good people leave a project.
whyNot.3: Low morale and stress are typical results of poor leadership.

B.q: A housing association's project manager works in a matrix organisation and has no line authority over the surveyors on her team. Why does leadership matter MORE than usual for her?
options: She can simply instruct them as their line manager
Surveyors in a matrix never need any motivation
The sponsor will motivate the team on her behalf
She must rely on influence rather than authority
B.why: In a matrix, team members still report to functional managers, so the PM has limited positional power and must lead through influence, clarity and trust.

whyNot.0: She has no line authority, so she cannot rely on instructing them as a line manager would.
whyNot.1: Everyone's motivation is affected by leadership, whatever the structure.
whyNot.2: The sponsor gives direction and support at a senior level; day-to-day team leadership is the PM's job.

B.q: A tester on a payroll system project finds a critical defect early, saving weeks of rework. Which response from the project manager is MOST likely to sustain her motivation?
options: Specific thanks for the early find and its effect
A general 'good job, everyone' at the month end
No comment, since finding defects is her job
Praise held back until the lessons learned report
B.why: Recognition works best when it is specific, timely and linked to the outcome it achieved. It also signals that raising problems early is valued.

whyNot.1: Generic, delayed praise doesn't connect the recognition to her particular contribution.
whyNot.2: Ignoring good work removes a powerful motivator and can discourage early reporting.
whyNot.3: Feedback weeks or months later loses most of its effect; timeliness matters.

B.q: An iterative team building a mobile banking feature is expected to self-organise. Which behaviour from the project manager BEST fits this way of working?
options: Allocating each task daily and checking it personally
Deciding the technical design alone to save time
Facilitating the team and removing its blockers
Waiting for the end-of-phase report to give feedback
B.why: In iterative delivery the team decides how to do the work; the PM leads by facilitating, clearing obstacles and protecting the team so it can deliver each iteration.

whyNot.0: Allocating and checking every task undermines self-organisation and ownership.
whyNot.1: Deciding the design alone removes the team's ownership of how the work is done.
whyNot.3: Iterative work relies on frequent feedback every iteration, not end-of-phase reports.

C.q: A software company's project manager responds to a slipping deadline by driving the team with criticism and warnings about consequences. Output rises for two sprints, then falls sharply as two developers resign. What BEST explains this pattern?
options: The team has moved into the performing stage early
Fear bought short-term compliance, not commitment
The backlog was prioritised badly by the product owner
Higher pressure always raises performance in the end
C.why: Pressure-led leadership can produce a short burst of compliance, but it erodes morale and commitment, so performance falls and people leave.

whyNot.0: Performing teams are stable and need little direction; resignations and falling output are not signs of performing.
whyNot.2: Nothing in the scenario points to backlog priorities; the change followed the shift in leadership behaviour.
whyNot.3: The scenario shows the opposite: pressure gave a short gain, then a sharper loss.

C.q:
Which TWO behaviours would MOST help a project manager improve team motivation?
1. Explaining how each task contributes to the project's purpose
2. Personally checking all work before it is released
3. Giving timely, specific feedback on contributions
4. Holding back information until decisions are final
options: 1 and 2
2 and 4
2 and 3
1 and 3
C.why: Connecting work to purpose (1) and giving timely, specific feedback (3) both build motivation and commitment.

whyNot.0: Checking all work personally (2) signals distrust and reduces ownership.
whyNot.1: Both 2 and 4 damage motivation: over-control and withholding information reduce trust.
whyNot.2: 3 helps, but 2 (checking everything personally) undermines ownership.

C.q: Two project managers lead similar teams with the same skills. PM A sets clear goals, explains why they matter and involves the team in planning. PM B issues instructions with no explanation. What is the MOST likely difference in results?
options: Team A shows more commitment and raises issues sooner
Team B performs better because instructions are clearer
There is no difference because the skills are the same
Team A needs far more supervision than Team B does
C.why: With the same skills, leadership is the difference. Clarity of purpose and involvement build commitment and an open climate where problems are raised early.

whyNot.1: Instructions without purpose or involvement tend to produce compliance rather than commitment.
whyNot.2: Skills set what people CAN do; leadership strongly affects what they WANT to do.
whyNot.3: Involved, committed teams usually need less supervision, not more.

reteach.title: Think of two football managers
reteach.question: Two managers take over identical squads. One shouts from the touchline and blames players after every loss; the other explains the game plan, involves senior players and praises effort. Which squad improves, and why?

blocks.body: Manager A's players stop taking risks: nobody wants the blame, so they pass sideways and hide. Mistakes are covered up rather than discussed. Manager B's players understand the plan, feel trusted to make decisions on the pitch and own their errors at training. Over a season, B's squad improves and A's stalls, with the same talent. A project team works the same way: leadership sets the climate, and the climate sets the performance.

blocks.text: Shouting louder is not leading better. Pressure can win one match; commitment wins the season.

explain.body: Leadership sets vision and direction, influences and aligns people towards a common purpose, and empowers and inspires them to succeed. Management plans, organises and controls. A project manager does both, but leadership is what earns people's willing effort.

test.q: Which BEST describes leadership in a project context?
options: Producing the schedule, budget and risk register
Holding formal line authority over team members
Setting direction and inspiring people to deliver
Approving the business case at each decision gate
test.why: Leadership is about direction, influence and inspiration: getting people committed to the common purpose.

whyNot.0: Producing plans and registers is management activity.
whyNot.1: Leadership doesn't depend on line authority; PMs often lead without it.
whyNot.3: Approving the business case is a sponsor and governance responsibility.

explain.body: Leader behaviour shapes the team climate (trust, clarity, safety to speak up). The climate drives motivation, morale and commitment. Those drive performance: quality, pace, ideas and how early problems are raised.

test.q: In the chain from leader behaviour to project results, what sits directly between the team climate and team performance?
options: Contract terms and penalty clauses
Motivation, morale and commitment
The sponsor's business case
Configuration management records
test.why: The climate a leader creates affects how motivated and committed people are, and that drives how well they perform.

whyNot.0: Contract terms are fixed agreements; they don't explain the link between climate and performance.
whyNot.2: The business case justifies the project; it is not the link between climate and performance.
whyNot.3: Configuration records control versions of deliverables, not people's performance.

explain.body: Blame, fear and over-control push people from commitment to compliance. Signs: problems hidden until formal reviews, capable people stop offering ideas, work is done to the letter and no more, stress rises and people leave. The cost shows up as delays, rework and poor decisions.

rows.label: Team asks to own more decisions

test.q: On a council's waste collection project, team members start working strictly to the letter of their roles and avoid anything extra. What does this MOST suggest?
options: Their skills have grown well beyond the task
The project has entered the transition phase
The schedule has too much float in every task
Commitment has dropped to bare compliance
test.why: Doing only the minimum is a classic sign that leadership has lost the team's discretionary effort and commitment.

whyNot.0: Growing skills usually show up as more initiative, not less.
whyNot.1: Transition is about handover; it doesn't explain a change in people's willingness.
whyNot.2: Float is a scheduling concept and doesn't explain reduced engagement.

explain.body: In a linear life cycle the PM plans, directs and coordinates work packages, using milestones and clear roles to motivate. In an iterative life cycle the self-organising team decides how to work, so the PM facilitates, removes blockers and builds motivation through autonomy and visible progress each iteration.

test.q: How does the project manager's leadership role typically differ in an iterative life cycle compared with a linear one?
options: More facilitating; the team decides how to do the work
More directive; the PM assigns every task each day
No different; style is fixed by the life cycle chosen
Absent; the product owner leads the whole team instead
test.why: Iterative teams self-organise around each iteration's goal, so the PM leads by facilitating and removing obstacles.

whyNot.1: Assigning every task daily conflicts with self-organisation.
whyNot.2: The life cycle doesn't fix one style; the emphasis changes with the way of working.
whyNot.3: The product owner prioritises the backlog; leadership of the team doesn't disappear.
